raw_evidence.label: Independent confirmation: the pace is breaking eval cycles
raw_evidence.content: External trackers corroborate the acceleration and add a 'so what'. Industry coverage in 2026 notes that frontier labs are 'releasing new models faster than ever', with the three leading labs now updating flagship models 'every few weeks, not every few months' — to the point that the pace itself is becoming a barrier to entry for smaller competitors. This is the real-world stake behind the median-gap numbers.

raw_evidence.label: The 30x cadence collapse: median gap fell from 132 to 4 days

The decline is monotonic across the clean era: 132 days (2018), 51 (2019), 68.5 (2020), 49 (2021), then a cliff to 13 (2022), 5.5 (2023), 7 (2024), and 4 (2025-26). In 2018 the frontier collectively shipped a notable language model roughly every four-and-a-half months; by 2025 it was shipping one every four days.

raw_evidence.label: Independent confirmation: the pace is breaking eval cycles
raw_evidence.content: External trackers corroborate the acceleration and add a 'so what'. Industry coverage in 2026 notes that frontier labs are 'releasing new models faster than ever', with the three leading labs now updating flagship models 'every few weeks, not every few months' — to the point that the pace itself is becoming a barrier to entry for smaller competitors. A Frontier Model Release Velocity Index reported roughly 12+ substantive frontier releases in Q1 2026 versus 6 in Q4 2025, a sustained pace near three meaningful launches per week. The downstream consequence: organizations that historically ran six-month model-evaluation cycles are being forced onto roughly four-week cadences, because the top model on a router like OpenRouter can change two or three times within a single quarter. This is the real-world stake behind the median-gap numbers.

raw_evidence.label: The 30x cadence collapse: median gap fell from 132 to 4 days
raw_evidence.content: The single defining finding: the median number of days between consecutive frontier-lab language-model releases collapsed from 132 days in 2018 to just 4 days in 2025 and 2026 (year-to-date) — a 33x speed-up. The decline is monotonic across the clean era: 132 days (2018), 51 (2019), 68.5 (2020), 49 (2021), then a cliff to 13 (2022), 5.5 (2023), 7 (2024), and 4 (2025-26). In 2018 the frontier collectively shipped a notable language model roughly every four-and-a-half months; by 2025 it was shipping one every four days.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_02: The 2022 cliff (ChatGPT-year inflection) ---
print("\n=== ana_02 ===")
m2021 = cad.loc[cad.year == 2021, "median_days_between_releases"].iloc[0]
m2022 = cad.loc[cad.year == 2022, "median_days_between_releases"].iloc[0]
m2023 = cad.loc[cad.year == 2023, "median_days_between_releases"].iloc[0]
print(f"2021 median gap: {m2021} days")
print(f"2022 median gap: {m2022} days (factor vs 2021: {m2021/m2022:.1f}x faster)")
print(f"2023 median gap: {m2023} days")
print(f"2021->2023 compression: {m2021/m2023:.1f}x")
raw_evidence.output:
2018: median 132.0 days, n=3
2019: median 51.0 days, n=4
2020: median 68.5 days, n=4
2021: median 49.0 days, n=8
2022: median 13.0 days, n=21
2023: median 5.5 days, n=26
2024: median 7.0 days, n=33
2025: median 4.0 days, n=54
2026: median 4.0 days, n=15

raw_evidence.content: The headline 30x speed-up is real but must be read carefully. Part of the cadence collapse comes from more labs entering the race and from point-releases and variants ('4.1', '4.5', 'Pro', 'Heavy', 'Thinking' editions) each clearing the notability bar as separate entries. That is itself part of the iteration-speed phenomenon being measured — labs ship smaller, more frequent increments — but it means a single 'release' today represents a smaller capability jump than a flagship release in 2019. The median-gap metric is robust to the partial 2026 year (data runs through mid-May, so 2026's annual COUNT is incomplete, but its gap of ~4 days is unaffected). Pre-2017 years have tiny sample sizes and noisy gap values that should be ignored; the clean trend runs 2019 to present.

raw_evidence.label: Scope suggestion for the Analyst
raw_evidence.content: The cleanest story lives in two derived tables. (1) frontier_cadence_by_year.csv: the field-wide median days between consecutive Language-domain frontier releases, bucketed by year — this is the headline metric and is the most defensible because the median is robust to the partial 2026 year and to outliers. (2) frontier_release_gaps.csv: within-lab release-to-release gaps for each of the named frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google/Google DeepMind/DeepMind, Meta AI, xAI, DeepSeek, Mistral AI, Alibaba), which lets you show that individual labs follow the same pattern, not just the pooled field. models_per_year.csv (annual notable-model volume) supports the macro 'more models overall' backdrop but its 2026 value is partial and must be flagged. Focus the analysis on 2018->2026 for cadence and treat pre-2017 gaps as noise.

Industry coverage in 2026 notes that frontier labs are 'releasing new models faster than ever', with the three leading labs now updating flagship models 'every few weeks, not every few months' — to the point that the pace itself is becoming a barrier to entry for smaller competitors. A Frontier Model Release Velocity Index reported roughly 12+ substantive frontier releases in Q1 2026 versus 6 in Q4 2025, a sustained pace near three meaningful launches per week. The downstream consequence: organizations that historically ran six-month model-evaluation cycles are being forced onto roughly four-week cadences, because the top model on a router like OpenRouter can change two or three times within a single quarter. This is the real-world stake behind the median-gap numbers.

raw_evidence.label: Anthropic's Claude line: from 4-month gaps to weeks
raw_evidence.content: Anthropic's own release log mirrors the field. Early Claude releases were months apart — Claude 2 came 119 days after the prior release, Claude 2.1 another 133 days, with a 2023 median of about 126 days. By late 2025 the gaps shrank to weeks: Claude Sonnet 4.5 followed Opus 4.1 by 55 days, Claude Haiku 4.5 came just 16 days later, and Claude Opus 4.5 another 40 days after that. The 0-day entries (Claude 3 Opus and 3 Sonnet on the same day; Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 on the same day) show simultaneous multi-model launches — a newer pattern in itself. This confirms the detective's external benchmark that Anthropic moved from ~120-day to 16–55-day cadences.

raw_evidence.content: External trackers corroborate the acceleration and add a 'so what'. Industry coverage in 2026 notes that frontier labs are 'releasing new models faster than ever', with the three leading labs now updating flagship models 'every few weeks, not every few months' — to the point that the pace itself is becoming a barrier to entry for smaller competitors. A Frontier Model Release Velocity Index reported roughly 12+ substantive frontier releases in Q1 2026 versus 6 in Q4 2025, a sustained pace near three meaningful launches per week. The downstream consequence: organizations that historically ran six-month model-evaluation cycles are being forced onto roughly four-week cadences, because the top model on a router like OpenRouter can change two or three times within a single quarter. This is the real-world stake behind the median-gap numbers.
